title: Allocation churn, heap region mapping, and OOM postmortem
content:
Summary:

This note captures the postmortem for the OOM incidents that caused several production serving nodes to fail during a high-throughput spike on 2026-01-21. Root cause is allocation churn on the device allocator combined with small-region fragmentation that prevented large workspace allocations from succeeding even when free memory (sum) appeared sufficient. We traced the failure to a behavioral pattern of the allocator cache + fallback cudaMalloc path and to transient tail-latencies in cudaMalloc that caused upstream backpressure to pile onto in-flight allocations.

High-level timeline:
- 2026-01-21 03:12 UTC: Traffic spike from a customer test increases inference concurrency and average sequence length.
- 03:13:12: First failed request observed (OOM in model forward while reserving workspace).
- 03:13:17–03:15: Several nodes entered degraded state; automatic fallback to smaller model variant triggered for some tenants.
- 03:20:00: SRE evicted affected worker pods; cluster recovered after rolling restart.

What we observed (evidence):
- GPU memory monitoring showed aggregate free memory ~18–22% on affected machines, but requests requiring contiguous workspace > 2.2GB failed.
- cudaMalloc traces (LD_PRELOAD logging + driver event hooks) show repeated small frees and allocs in the 32KB–2MB range interleaved with a few large frees.
- The allocator used (custom pooling layer on top of CUDA driver with a per-device LRU cache) kept many small regions live; virtual address space became fragmented across multiple regions. The allocator attempted to satisfy a large 2.5GB allocation by scanning free lists and failing because no single contiguous region large enough existed.
- When the pool scan failed, code fell back to direct cudaMalloc. In some cases, cudaMalloc returned ENOMEM or experienced >100ms latency. The combination of failed attempts and retries caused the request pipeline to keep more allocations outstanding, worsening fragmentation.
- jemalloc/ptmalloc hooks in host process showed high allocation churn in the host-side data structures used to stage GPU tensors (particularly in the quantize/dequantize path for mixed-precision reshaping).

Root causes (detailed):
1) Allocation churn + many short-lived small device allocations
   - Several components (attention kv-cache maintenance, temp buffers for layer norm and softmax) allocate scratch buffers per-layer per-batch rather than reusing a pre-sized workspace. Under normal load this was fine; under high concurrency it produced heavy churn in the pool which amplified fragmentation.

2) Pool design that fragments across small regions
   - The pooling strategy segments allocations into same-size buckets, but when object sizes vary it keeps adjacent small free blocks rather than coalescing into larger spans. No periodic compaction.

3) Fallback path to cudaMalloc synchronous call
   - When the pool cannot satisfy an allocation the runtime falls back to cudaMalloc. This path has higher latency and occasionally fails when the device is fragmented even if total free memory is large. We relied on retries that further increased pressure.

4) Workload shift to longer sequences and higher concurrency
   - The distribution of sequence lengths changed: median length up ~1.6x, tail length up ~2.5x. That pushed per-request workspace requirements across bucket boundaries, increasing probability of requiring a large contiguous allocation.

5) Interplay with host memory churn
   - Host-side staging allocs and short-lived buffers (jemalloc churn) delayed frees and reorderings of GPU frees in callback threads, increasing time that small regions remained allocated.

Reproduction notes / profiling artifacts:
- Reproduction script: run load-generator with 300 concurrent sessions, mixed seq lengths 32/128/512 with percentiles [50,90,99] = [32,128,512]. Increase ramp over 30s. This reproduces fragmentation in ~8–12 minutes on prod-like instance type (A100-80GB, CUDA 12.x).
- Collected traces: GPU memory map snapshots every 5s (nvidia-smi --query), LD_PRELOAD cudaMalloc intercept logs, and allocator internal free-list dumps. Attached logs referenced in linked_artifacts.
- Useful command pipeline to inspect per-region fragmentation (on a host with allocator debug enabled):
  - cat /proc/<pid>/maps | grep -i cuda; use our allocator dump tool: ./tools/alloc-dump --pid <pid> --format region-holes
- Histogram observed: heavy counts in small sizes (<=256KB) and a long tail of interspersed 1–4MB allocs; free ranges that would be needed for a 2.2GB allocation were present in sum but split across ~160 pockets.

Mitigations attempted during incident:
- Forced eviction of idle caches (runtime API): freed many small buffers and temporarily resolved a subset of failures. This was manual and slow.
- Temporarily disabled retries in the fallback path so failures surfaced earlier and backpressure propagated to the front-end, preventing buildup of concurrent in-flight allocation attempts. This reduced propagation but increased failed requests.

Short-term mitigations (we implemented):
- Add an aggressive per-device periodic compaction call that coalesces adjacent free spans in the pool during low-util windows (implemented and rolled to canary 2026-01-29).
- Change fallback behavior: instead of synchronous retries on cudaMalloc failure, trigger immediate graceful degradation (route to smaller model variant) and schedule a background async compaction before attempting one last direct allocation.
- Increase default workspace pre-allocation for long-sequence requests: allocate a pinned pre-reserved workspace per-executor sized to 75th percentile request instead of per-layer micro-allocations. This reduces churn for many workloads.

Long-term fixes and design proposals:
1) Move to a slab allocator with coalescing and support for large-span reservations
   - Design a two-tier allocator: small-slab fast path with fixed-size bins for <=1MB objects, and a large-span manager that maintains coalesced regions and supports contiguous reservations for large workspaces.

2) Adopt cudaMallocAsync-based fast-path with explicit space reservation
   - CUDA 11.6+ exposes cudaMallocAsync and memory pools; integrate this into runtime to let driver manage fragmentation and reuse more efficiently. Requires fallback path and policy to fall back to driver pools when fragmentation threshold exceeded.

3) Allocation-aware scheduling and backpressure
   - Add scheduling primitives that account for in-flight allocation footprint. Avoid letting many requests simultaneously reserve large workspaces; instead serialize or reduce concurrency when free contiguous spans are low.

4) Telemetry improvements
   - Emit per-request maximum contiguous-free-span metric (sampled) and allocator fragmentation ratio (largest_free_span / total_free). Add alerting when ratio falls below threshold on any worker.

5) Host-side latency reduction
   - Reduce host-side jemalloc churn by reusing staging buffers and using thread-local caches for host buffers that participate in GPU staging to reduce delayed frees.

Action items (owners + ETA):
- Priya Shah: finalize and land periodic compaction code and unit tests (ETA 2026-02-05) [DONE on canary].
- Samira Patel: implement graceful-degrade-on-alloc-failure policy and integration test harness (ETA 2026-02-14).
- Luca Bianchi: prototype cudaMallocAsync integration branch and benchmark vs current (ETA 2026-03-01).
- Jordan Kim: add allocator fragmentation telemetry and Grafana dashboard prototype (ETA 2026-02-21).

Open questions / tradeoffs we debated:
- Frequency and CPU cost of compaction: compaction scans are not free. We tuned to run at low-util windows and made it interruptible. Need more stress testing.
- How aggressive to be with automatic model downshift: conservative downshift reduces user-facing errors but increases per-request latency/quality change. We default to a policy that only downshifts for ephemeral spikes, not for sustained load.
- Rely on driver (cudaMallocAsync) vs keep user-space pooling: driver pools are attractive but reduce observability and control. We should benchmark for tail-latency and fragmentation under mixed workloads.

Appendix: quick debugging checklist for on-call
- Check nvidia-smi memory summary vs allocator largest-free-span metric. If largest_free_span < expected workspace size, suspect fragmentation.
- Dump allocator free-lists: ./tools/alloc-dump --pid <pid> --format holes 
- If fragmentation present: trigger runtime cache eviction: POST /runtime/admin/evict-caches -> frees small buffers.
- If many cudaMalloc slow calls: inspect driver version and kernel logs; consider restarting affected worker after snapshot.

Concluding note:
This incident surfaced a classically under-appreciated failure mode: aggregate free memory is a poor signal for the ability to satisfy contiguous workspace allocations. Our path forward combines allocator improvements, adoption of driver-side async alloc APIs, and run-time scheduling changes to keep tail fragmentation from turning into customer-impacting OOMs.
